sections.title: Present Tense: Regular Verbs
sections.rule: Drop the infinitive ending (-ar/-er/-ir) and add the personal endings. -ar: -o/-as/-a/-amos/-áis/-an; -er: -o/-es/-e/-emos/-éis/-en; -ir: -o/-es/-e/-imos/-ís/-en. Subject pronouns are usually omitted because the ending shows the person.
sections.example_target: Hablo español y estudio todos los días.
sections.example_target_2: ¿Dónde vives ahora?
sections.example_ref: English: I speak Spanish and study every day. / Where do you live now?
sections.note: -er and -ir verbs share endings except in nosotros/vosotros (comemos vs. vivimos, coméis vs. vivís).

sections.title: Ser vs Estar
sections.rule: Both mean 'to be'. Use ser for permanent traits, identity, origin, time and profession (soy médico, es de México). Use estar for temporary states, feelings and location (estoy cansado, está en casa).
sections.example_target: Ella es española, pero ahora está en Francia.
sections.example_target_2: La sopa está fría y el hielo es frío.
sections.example_ref: English: She is Spanish, but right now she is in France. / The soup is (has gotten) cold and ice is (inherently) cold.
sections.note: Some adjectives change meaning: ser aburrido = boring, estar aburrido = bored; ser listo = clever, estar listo = ready.

sections.title: Preterite Tense
sections.rule: The preterite narrates completed past actions. Regular -ar: -é/-aste/-ó/-amos/-asteis/-aron; -er/-ir: -í/-iste/-ió/-imos/-isteis/-ieron. Key irregulars: ser/ir share fui/fuiste/fue; hacer→hice/hizo; tener→tuve; estar→estuve.
sections.example_target: Ayer comí paella y bebí vino tinto.
sections.example_target_2: Fuimos al cine y volvimos tarde.
sections.example_ref: English: Yesterday I ate paella and drank red wine. / We went to the cinema and came back late.
sections.note: Ser and ir look identical in the preterite; context tells them apart (fui médico = I was a doctor / fui a casa = I went home).

sections.title: Imperfect Tense
sections.rule: The imperfect describes habitual, repeated or ongoing past actions ('used to', 'was ...-ing'). -ar: -aba/-abas/-aba/-ábamos/-abais/-aban; -er/-ir: -ía/-ías/-ía/-íamos/-íais/-ían. Only three irregulars: ser (era), ir (iba), ver (veía).
sections.example_target: Cuando era niño, jugaba en el parque cada tarde.
sections.example_target_2: Llovía mientras leíamos.
sections.example_ref: English: When I was a child, I used to play in the park every afternoon. / It was raining while we were reading.
sections.note: Use the imperfect for the background scene and the preterite for the single event that interrupts it: leía cuando sonó el teléfono.

sections.title: Reflexive Verbs
sections.rule: Reflexive verbs take a pronoun (me/te/se/nos/os/se) that matches the subject and normally comes before the conjugated verb. They express actions done to oneself: levantarse, llamarse, sentirse.
sections.example_target: Me levanto a las siete y me ducho.
sections.example_target_2: ¿Cómo te llamas?
sections.example_ref: English: I get up at seven and take a shower. / What is your name (what do you call yourself)?
sections.note: With an infinitive or gerund the pronoun may attach to the end: voy a levantarme / me voy a levantar are both correct.

sections.title: Object Pronouns
sections.rule: Direct object pronouns (lo/la/los/las) replace the thing acted on; indirect object pronouns (me/te/le/nos/os/les) mark the recipient. Both go before the conjugated verb.
sections.example_target: ¿El libro? Lo leí anoche.
sections.example_target_2: Le di las flores a mi madre.
sections.example_ref: English: The book? I read it last night. / I gave the flowers to my mother.
sections.note: Le/les often appear even when the recipient is named ('le di ... a mi madre'); this redundant pronoun is normal and correct in Spanish.

sections.title: Present Subjunctive
sections.rule: Formed from the yo present stem plus 'opposite' endings: -ar verbs take -e endings, -er/-ir verbs take -a endings (hable, coma, viva). Used after expressions of wish, emotion, doubt and with 'cuando' about the future.
sections.example_target: Quiero que vengas a la fiesta.
sections.example_target_2: Ojalá que haga buen tiempo mañana.
sections.example_ref: English: I want you to come to the party. / I hope the weather is good tomorrow.
sections.note: Irregular yo-forms carry into the subjunctive: tener→tenga, hacer→haga, salir→salga. Six verbs are fully irregular: sea, esté, vaya, dé, sepa, haya.

sections.title: Future Tense
sections.rule: Add one set of endings to the whole infinitive: -é/-ás/-á/-emos/-éis/-án. Irregular verbs change only the stem, not the endings: tener→tendr-, poder→podr-, hacer→har-, decir→dir-, salir→saldr-.
sections.example_target: Mañana viajaré a Sevilla.
sections.example_target_2: Tendremos que esperar un poco.
sections.example_ref: English: Tomorrow I will travel to Seville. / We will have to wait a while.
sections.note: The future can express probability about the present: ¿Qué hora será? = I wonder what time it is (it must be...).

sections.title: Por vs Para
sections.rule: Para points forward: purpose, destination, deadline, recipient (estudio para aprender, salgo para Madrid). Por points to cause, exchange, duration and 'through/along' (gracias por todo, pagué diez euros por el libro).
sections.example_target: Este regalo es para ti; lo compré por veinte euros.
sections.example_target_2: Caminamos por el parque para llegar más rápido.
sections.example_ref: English: This gift is for you; I bought it for twenty euros. / We walked through the park in order to get there faster.
sections.note: 'Thank you for' is always gracias por; 'in order to' + verb is always para: para comer, para estudiar.

sections.title: Present Perfect
sections.rule: Formed with the present of haber (he/has/ha/hemos/habéis/han) plus the past participle (-ado for -ar, -ido for -er/-ir). It links a past action to the present, often with hoy, ya, todavía, alguna vez.
sections.example_target: Hoy he comido demasiado.
sections.example_target_2: ¿Alguna vez has estado en España?
sections.example_ref: English: Today I have eaten too much. / Have you ever been to Spain?
sections.note: Common irregular participles: hacer→hecho, decir→dicho, ver→visto, escribir→escrito, volver→vuelto, poner→puesto. The participle never changes for gender here.

sections.title: Conditional Tense
sections.rule: Add -ía/-ías/-ía/-íamos/-íais/-ían to the infinitive to say 'would'. It uses the same irregular stems as the future (tendría, podría, haría). Used for hypotheticals, polite requests and future-in-the-past.
sections.example_target: Yo viajaría por todo el mundo si pudiera.
sections.example_target_2: ¿Podrías ayudarme, por favor?
sections.example_ref: English: I would travel all over the world if I could. / Could you help me, please?
sections.note: Conditional endings are identical to imperfect -er/-ir endings, but they attach to the full infinitive: comería, not comía.

sections.title: Imperative (Commands)
sections.rule: Affirmative tú uses the third-person present (habla, come, vive); formal usted and all negative commands use the subjunctive (hable, no hables, no coma). Pronouns attach to affirmative commands and precede negative ones.
sections.example_target: Habla más despacio, por favor.
sections.example_target_2: No lo hagas; dámelo a mí.
sections.example_ref: English: Speak more slowly, please. / Don't do it; give it to me.
sections.note: Eight irregular affirmative tú commands: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven. Adding a pronoun often needs a written accent: dímelo, hazlo.

sections.title: Comparatives & Superlatives
sections.rule: Comparisons use más/menos + adjective + que (more/less ... than) or tan + adjective + como (as ... as). The superlative adds a definite article: el/la/los/las más/menos + adjective + de.
sections.example_target: Mi hermano es más alto que yo.
sections.example_target_2: Es la ciudad más bonita de España.
sections.example_ref: English: My brother is taller than I am. / It is the most beautiful city in Spain.
sections.note: Irregular forms replace más + adjective: bueno→mejor, malo→peor, grande→mayor, pequeño→menor. Note 'in/of' after a superlative is de, not en.

sections.title: Gustar-Type Verbs
sections.rule: Gustar means 'to be pleasing', so the thing liked is the subject and the person is an indirect object: me/te/le/nos/os/les + gusta (singular) or gustan (plural thing). Same pattern: encantar, interesar, doler, faltar.
sections.example_target: Me gusta el café pero me gustan más los tés.
sections.example_target_2: A los niños les encantan los dulces.
sections.example_ref: English: I like coffee but I like teas more. / The children love sweets.
sections.note: Use gusta before a singular noun or a verb (me gusta bailar) and gustan before a plural noun. The clarifying 'a + person' is optional but common: a mí me gusta.

sections.title: Present Progressive
sections.rule: Formed with estar + the gerund (-ando for -ar, -iendo for -er/-ir) to stress an action happening right now. Some gerunds are irregular: leer→leyendo, dormir→durmiendo, pedir→pidiendo.
sections.example_target: Estoy escribiendo un correo ahora mismo.
sections.example_target_2: Los niños están durmiendo.
sections.example_ref: English: I am writing an email right now. / The children are sleeping.
sections.note: Unlike English, Spanish does not use the progressive for future plans; say voy al cine mañana, not estoy yendo. Object pronouns may attach: estoy leyéndolo / lo estoy leyendo.

sections.title: Relative Pronouns
sections.rule: Que ('that/which/who') is the all-purpose relative. Use quien/quienes for people after a preposition, el que/el cual for clarity, and cuyo/cuya ('whose') to show possession. Lo que means 'what/that which'.
sections.example_target: El libro que leí es de un autor cuya obra admiro.
sections.example_target_2: La mujer con quien hablé es mi jefa.
sections.example_ref: English: The book that I read is by an author whose work I admire. / The woman with whom I spoke is my boss.
sections.note: Cuyo agrees with the thing possessed, not the possessor: el hombre cuyas hijas conozco (whose daughters). Never use 'de quien' where cuyo fits.

sections.title: Double Object Pronouns
sections.rule: When both an indirect and a direct object pronoun appear, the indirect comes first. Crucially, le/les becomes se before lo/la/los/las to avoid two l-sounds.
sections.example_target: ¿El regalo? Se lo di a Juan ayer.
sections.example_target_2: ¿Me lo puedes traer? / ¿Puedes traérmelo?
sections.example_ref: English: The gift? I gave it to him yesterday. / Can you bring it to me?
sections.note: Se lo/se la is ambiguous, so a clarifier is often added: se lo di a ella. When both attach to an infinitive, add an accent: traérmelo.

sections.title: Past Perfect (Pluscuamperfecto)
sections.rule: Formed with the imperfect of haber (había/habías/había/habíamos/habíais/habían) plus the past participle. It describes an action completed before another past moment.
sections.example_target: Cuando llegué, la película ya había empezado.
sections.example_target_2: No fui porque ya había comido.
sections.example_ref: English: When I arrived, the film had already started. / I didn't go because I had already eaten.
sections.note: It is the clearest tense for sequencing past events: the pluscuamperfecto action always happens first. Ya ('already') is a frequent companion.

sections.title: Passive Voice
sections.rule: The true passive uses ser + past participle, which agrees in gender and number, with the agent introduced by por (la casa fue construida por ellos). In everyday Spanish the passive/impersonal se is far more common: se venden coches, se habla español.
sections.example_target: La novela fue escrita en 1955.
sections.example_target_2: Aquí se hablan tres idiomas.
sections.example_ref: English: The novel was written in 1955. / Three languages are spoken here.
sections.note: Prefer the se-passive when the agent is unknown or unimportant; the ser-passive sounds formal or journalistic. The verb after se agrees with the noun: se vende / se venden.

sections.title: Future Perfect
sections.rule: Formed with the future of haber (habré/habrás/habrá/habremos/habréis/habrán) plus the past participle. It marks an action that will be finished by a future point, and can also express probability about the recent past.
sections.example_target: Para las cinco habré terminado el informe.
sections.example_target_2: Ya habrá salido de casa.
sections.example_ref: English: By five o'clock I will have finished the report. / He has probably already left home.
sections.note: 'By/before a deadline' is para: para mañana habremos acabado. The probability use ('must have') is very common in speech.

sections.title: Imperfect Subjunctive
sections.rule: Formed from the third-person plural preterite (ellos) minus -ron, plus -ra or -se endings (hablara/hablase, comiera/comiese, fuera/fuese). Used after past-tense triggers and in hypothetical 'si' clauses.
sections.example_target: Quería que vinieras a la boda.
sections.example_target_2: Si tuviera dinero, viajaría más.
sections.example_ref: English: I wanted you to come to the wedding. / If I had money, I would travel more.
sections.note: The -ra and -se forms are interchangeable, though -ra is more common in speech. Any irregular preterite stem carries over: tener→tuviera, ir/ser→fuera.

sections.title: Conditional Perfect & Third Conditional
sections.rule: The conditional perfect is habría + participle ('would have'). It pairs with si + past perfect subjunctive (hubiera + participle) to talk about unreal past situations and regrets.
sections.example_target: Si hubiera sabido, habría venido antes.
sections.example_target_2: Habríamos ganado con un poco más de suerte.
sections.example_ref: English: If I had known, I would have come earlier. / We would have won with a bit more luck.
sections.note: In casual speech the hubiera form is sometimes used in both clauses (si hubiera sabido, hubiera venido), but the textbook pairing is hubiera ... habría.
